title: Usage
description: Get the TaktX engine running within a few minutes
text: Getting started with the beta version TaktX has reached public beta phase. Join us in testing and evaluation and experience the high throughput performance that TaktX provides. Note, the engine and client are not feature complete and subject to change, but we are getting more stable. We use this period to get some battle experience and improve quality and performance based on your feedback. Prerequisites Note the following prerequisites to run the engine: Understand the license terms of the public beta phase Docker & Docker compose Have a running Kafka installation (included with the docker compose installation) JDK 21+ with Maven or Gradle to run the client Camunda Desktop Modeler to create your models Run TaktX with Docker Compose To start a complete TaktX environment locally: Download the artifact for TaktX Docker Compose , then extract it. In the extracted directory in a terminal, run: docker compose --profile full up -d Wait for the environment to initialize. Monitor the logs to ensure all components start. # show the running containers docker ps # Show the log of each container docker logs -f [Container id or name of the container] The default docker compose file will start the following components: Kafka for our persisted messages (port 9092) Kafka UI, manage the Kafka topics (port 8085) Grafana (port 3000) / Prometheus for metrics. It has a preconfigured dashboard The Taktx engine (port 8079( The Console containing Runway, to monitor and administer process instances (port 3002) After the applications have started succesfully you should see several topics being created in Kafka-UI. These topics are what drives the TaktX BPMN engine. All state is persisted in these topics. Open Runway by navigating to http://localhost:3002 Note: this docker compose file does not employ any authentication/authorisation so it is not recommended to run this in a production-like environment. Also it will not scale, for full scalability we will need an actual Kafka cluster and a separate set of Engine nodes Next up: creating and running TaktX clients

title: Engine
description: All information related to starting the engine
text: TaktX Engine — Deployment & Architecture Overview Overview TaktX is a lightweight BPMN engine built as a Java Quarkus application. It uses Apache Kafka as the single source of truth for persistence and storage and relies on Kafka topics to manage process definitions, process state and external tasks like service and send tasks. The engine is shipped today as a Docker image; plain JAR and native builds are planned for future releases. Kafka for persistence and storage All runtime state and task events are persisted to Kafka topics. Kafka acts as the durable event log and recovery store. Events and task messages are retained in Kafka so instances can replay stream data to reconstruct state after restarts or join the cluster at any time. Offset commits and topic durability provide recovery semantics: uncommitted work will be redelivered after consumer failure. External tasks and topic model External tasks (for example: service tasks, send tasks) are organized by job id. Each job id has its own Kafka topic. Topics are managed dynamically: when the engine detects a new job id it will create and start using a topic for that job id. The engine publishes task triggers into that per-job topic and worker instances consume from it. This isolates task types and simplifies routing and scaling. Topics are partitioned. Parallelism for a job id is achieved by adding partitions; each partition is consumed by at most one consumer instance in a consumer group. Deployment and distribution Implementation: Java + Quarkus. Current distribution: Docker image only. Run the image in your container platform and point it at your Kafka cluster, or use the provided docker-compose file which includes a Kafka installation Upcoming distributions: plain executable JAR and GraalVM native builds (smaller footprint and faster startup) will be provided in future releases. Horizontal scalability Scale-out model: run multiple TaktX engine instances that all connect to the same Kafka cluster. Per-job parallelism: increase the number of partitions on a job topic; add more engine instances. Kafka will assign partitions across instances, enabling concurrent processing of tasks for that job id. Work distribution: client instances join the same Kafka consumer group for a given job topic. Kafka’s partition assignment guarantees exclusive consumption per partition, avoiding duplicate concurrent processing of the same partition. Recommended practice: increase partitions to match desired parallelism and then add instances. Partitions are the unit of parallel work.

title: Client
description: All info related to creating and running clients
text: TaktX client libraries These sections describe how we can deploy BPMN files and run worker code using the TaktX client libraries. The TaktX client libraries provide access to the TaktX platform and allow to start and manipulate process instances, process definitions, listen to events etc. etc. We provide multiple ways to run the clients and we also provide convenience libraries for frameworks like Spring Boot and Quarkus. Find explanations on how to use these libraries in the subsections of this section. Also have a look at the examples repo

title: Vanilla taktx-client
description: Description of features of the vanilla taktx-client
text: Introduction The vanilla taktx-client contains all the functionality to communicate with the TaktX plaform. It allows you to deploy process definitions, start process instances, send messages and signals and even allows you to subscribe to the InstanceUpdateRecord stream to get deep insight into what happened with your flows. Maven/gradle dependency To start using it in a Java based application you need to add a gradle/maven dependency to the specific version of the taktx-client which is compatible with your TaktX platform. When using maven: <dependency> <groupId>io.taktx</groupId> <artifactId>taktx-client</artifactId> <version>0.4.0-beta-1</version> </dependency> When using gradle: implementation("io.taktx:taktx-client:0.4.0-beta-1") This will make sure the taktx-client and all transitive dependencies are included into your application. Creating the client object To create the client object a TaktClientBuilder has been introduced. Create an instance of the TaktXClient with the following: Properties taktProperties = new Properties(); TaktXClientBuilder taktClientBuilder = TaktXClient.newClientBuilder(); taktClient = taktClientBuilder.withTaktProperties(taktProperties).build(); taktClient.start(); The taktProperties will have to be filled with the correct configuration parameters. This should at least include the following properties. Enter the property values for your environment. bootstrap.servers=localhost:9092 taktx.engine.namespace=namespace There a lots more configuration parameters. See the Client Configuration section for the details. There are two ways on how to use the TaktXClient, first one is purely calling public API. The second one is by leveraging the power of annotations. Using the public API Once the TaktXClient has been started, you can use the public API to deploy process definitions, start process instances, send messages and signals and even subscribe to the event stream. For the full javadoc look here and look at github at the client-worker-vanilla-pure for an example implementation. Creating topics for external tasks Jobworkers rely on the existence of the corresponding topic for each job. The creation of these topics can be requested by the client as follows: Currently it is the engine that will respond to these requests by creating the corresponding Kafka topics. Deploying BPMN files Registering a jobworker Create class which implements the io.taktx.client.ExternalTaskTriggerConsumer interface. It will need to implement two methods: The getJobIds method should return the task-ids that this worker will support The acceptBatch method which will need to support all external task requests Using Annotations As described in the paragraphs above, you see that especially the worker implementation is a bit cumbersome. The client does provide an alternative and easier way to deploy BPMN resources and create and manage workers. This way the classpath is scanned for specific annotations and the client will make sure the correct wiring is in place. Look at github at the client-worker-vanilla-annotions for an example implementation. Deploying BPMN files To automatically deploy BPMN files we need to add the @Deployment annotation. For example on the main class or on a Configuration bean. By calling deployTaktDeploymentAnnotatedClasses on the TaktXClient all @Deployment annotations will be scanned and all corresponding BPMN files will be deployed automatically. Starting workers By registering the AnnotationScanningExternalTaskTriggerConsumer as externalTaskTriggerConsumer we can also scan the codebase automatically for @TaktWorkerMethod annotations and do all wiring automatically. The worker classes must have a default constructor so they can be instantiated by the PlainJavaInstanceProvider(). After that each worker method can be annotated by the JobWorker annotation and the variables and response will be mapped to/from in-engine variables automatically

title: Taktx-client-quarkus
description: The Quarkus wrapper around the taktx-client library
text: Introduction By using the taktx-client-quarkus wrapper library around the vanilla taktx-client the configuration and initialization of the taktx-client is done automatically. We can use the default Quarkus ways (like application properties) for configuration and the TaktXClient bean is initialized automatically. Maven/gradle dependency To start using it in a Java based application you need to add a gradle/maven dependency to the specific version of the taktx-client which is compatible with your TaktX platform. When using maven: <dependency> <groupId>io.taktx</groupId> <artifactId>taktx-client-quarkus</artifactId> <version>0.4.0-beta-1</version> </dependency> When using gradle: implementation("io.taktx:taktx-client0-quarkus:0.4.0-beta-1") During Quarkus initialization the code-base will be scanned for: @Deployment classes automatically upon startup and the corresponding BPMN files will be deployed @TaktWorkerMethod methods upon startup and the corresponding external task topics will be subscribed to Also during Quarkus initialization the code-base is scanner for Observer methods which observe InstanceUpdateRecord events. If there are any, a subscription is made to the TaktX engine event-stream and any incoming messages will be published. For an example, have a look in the GitHub example repo and look specifically for the client-workers-quarkus example. Deploying BPMN files To automatically deploy BPMN files we need to add the @Deployment annotation to a Quarkus bean. For example on the main class or on a Configuration bean. Starting workers Workers in Quarkus must be Application scoped beans and also annotated with the @Startup annotation to make sure they are instantiated. By adding @JobWorker annotations on methods the workers are automatically registered and subscribed to the corresponding external task topics.

title: Swagger UI Test client
description: Helpful to get started running process instances
text: If you are not using the console UI to manage your process definitions and process instances, you can use the client helper application which exposes an API with a Swagger page to do some basic operations. The application can be found in the examples repo and specifically in the client-swagger-ui subfolder. By cloning the repo you can start the application with the following command: ./gradlew -p client-swagger-ui quarkusDev By default the application is configured to connect to the kafka running at localhost:9092 When the application has started you can open the Swagger-ui at http://localhost:8082/q/swagger-ui/ This will show a Swagger UI which allows you to retrieve the deployed process definitions and start (batches of) process instances and pass a set of variables with it. Note that there is a difference in just starting a set of process instances and starting a job. The first will start the given number of process instances immediately. The latter one will start the given number of process instances every second. Jobs can also be changed and stopped by using the corresponding endpoints.

title: BPMN
text: Although the BPMN specification is standardized, it allows for vendor specific extensions which are heaviliy used by BPMN implementations. TaktX is initially made to be compatible with the extensions from Camunda 8 or Zeebe. So the best option to create BPMN models which run in TaktX is to download the Camunda Modeler here . When creating a new model make sure to select Camunda 8 to create the Taktx compatible BPMN files.

title: TaktX Engine architecture
description: This section and subsections explain the main concepts on how the TaktX engine architecture and design
text: TaktX Engine Overview What is TaktX? TaktX is a distributed, event-driven process orchestration engine built natively on Apache Kafka. It is designed for high scalability, resilience, and operational flexibility, making it suitable for modern cloud-native and microservices architectures. TaktX enables you to model, execute, and monitor complex business processes with fine-grained control and high throughput. Key Concepts Kafka-Centric Architecture: All communication and state management is handled via Kafka topics and Kafka Streams state stores. Engine Nodes: Stateless workers that process events and manage process state using Kafka Streams. Dynamic Topic Management: Topics are created on demand for job workers, user tasks, and process types, enabling fine-tuned scaling. Clients: Applications and services interact with TaktX exclusively through Kafka, submitting commands and consuming events. Extensibility: Plugins and custom integrations communicate via Kafka topics, making the system highly extensible. How TaktX Works When a client wants to start a process, it produces a message to a Kafka topic. Engine nodes, running as Kafka Streams applications, consume these messages, process them, and write results or follow-up events back to other topics. This pattern is consistent for all interactions, whether it’s starting a process, completing a user task, or handling a timer event. All state—process instances, variables, timers, and message subscriptions—is managed in Kafka Streams state stores, partitioned for scalability and resilience. Core Features Event-Driven Orchestration: All process execution and state changes are event-driven and durable. Fine-Grained State Access: State is loaded on demand, minimizing memory usage and maximizing throughput. Dynamic Scaling: Topics and partitions can be added as needed, allowing the system to scale horizontally. Resilience: Engine nodes are stateless and recoverable; state is restored from Kafka changelogs. Observability: Metrics, logs, and traces are available for monitoring and debugging. How TaktX Scales TaktX scales by partitioning both topics and state stores. Each engine node is responsible for a subset of partitions, and Kafka ensures that messages for a given key ( such as a process instance ID ) are routed to the correct node. As load increases, you can add more engine nodes and partitions to distribute the workload. How TaktX Handles Failures If an engine node fails, Kafka Streams automatically restores its state from the changelog topic. Other nodes can take over processing, ensuring minimal disruption. Because all communication is via Kafka, clients and other nodes are unaffected by individual node failures. How TaktX Persists Data All process state is stored in Kafka Streams state stores, which can be configured for in-memory or persisted storage. State changes are logged to Kafka changelogs, ensuring durability and recoverability. This approach allows for both high performance and strong consistency guarantees. Next Steps To learn more about each aspect of TaktX, see the following sections : Topics and Messaging Engine Nodes and State Stores Clients and API Job Workers and User Tasks Dynamic Topic Management State Management and Persistence Scaling and Partitioning Fault Tolerance and Recovery Observability and Operations Each section provides a deep dive into the concepts, design decisions, and implementation details, with diagrams and real-world examples.

title: Topics and messaging
text: Topics and Messaging In TaktX, Kafka topics are the backbone of all communication and state management. Every command, event, and data change flows through a Kafka topic, making the system highly decoupled and scalable. Let’s dive into how topics are used, how they’re managed, and why this approach is so powerful. The Role of Topics Think of a Kafka topic as a channel for a specific kind of message. For example, when a client wants to start a process, it sends a message to a dedicated topic. Engine nodes listen to these topics, process the messages, and emit results or follow-up events to other topics. This pattern is used for all interactions : process commands, job worker tasks, user tasks, and system events. Dynamic Topic Creation Unlike systems with a fixed set of channels, TaktX creates topics on demand. When a new job worker is registered, a topic is created specifically for it. This dynamic approach allows the system to scale horizontally and isolate workloads for performance tuning and monitoring. For example, if you have a high-throughput job worker, you can give it its own topic a larget partition count , ensuring it doesn’t compete for resources with other parts of the system. Partitioning for Scalability Each topic can be partitioned, which means its messages are distributed across multiple Kafka brokers and engine nodes. Partitioning is key to scaling : it allows many engine nodes to process messages in parallel, and ensures that related messages ( like those for a specific process instance ) are routed to the same partition for consistency. Message Flow Here’s how a typical message flows through the system : A client produces a command to a Kafka topic (e.g., start process). An engine node consumes the message, processes it, and updates state. The engine node emits events or results to other topics (e.g., process started, user task created). Other clients or engine nodes consume these events and react accordingly. This event-driven flow ensures that every action is durable, traceable, and can be replayed or audited if needed. Operational Considerations Kafka’s built-in tools make it easy to monitor topics, partitions, and consumer lag. TaktX leverages these features for observability and operational insight. In the future, a dedicated admin application will provide even more control over topic lifecycle and configuration.

title: Engine Nodes & State Stores
text: Engine Nodes and State Stores Engine nodes are the workers of the TaktX engine. They run as Kafka Streams applications, consuming messages from topics, processing them, and managing process state. Let’s look at how they work and how state is managed. Stateless by Design Engine nodes themselves are stateless—they don’t keep any long-term data in memory or on disk. Instead, all state is managed in Kafka Streams state stores, which are partitioned and distributed across the cluster. This design makes it easy to scale up and to recover from failures. State Stores: The Engine’s Memory Each engine node maintains local state stores for process instances, variables, timers, and message subscriptions. These stores can be configured for in-memory ( fast, volatile ) or persisted ( durable, larger ) storage. When a node processes an event, it loads only the relevant state from its local store, keeping memory usage low and performance high. Partition Assignment Kafka assigns partitions to engine nodes, ensuring that each node is responsible for a subset of the data. This partitioning is what enables horizontal scaling : as you add more nodes, Kafka redistributes partitions to balance the load. Recovery and Resilience If a node fails, Kafka Streams restores its state from the changelog topic. This makes the system highly resilient and minimizes downtime.

title: Clients & API
text: Clients and API Clients are the applications and services that interact with TaktX. They don’t connect to engine nodes directly—instead, they communicate exclusively via Kafka topics. This approach decouples clients from the engine, making the system more flexible and scalable. Submitting Commands To start a process, complete a task, or send an event, a client produces a message to the appropriate Kafka topic. The message format is well-defined, ensuring compatibility and traceability. Consuming Events Clients can subscribe to topics to receive updates about process execution, task assignments, and results. This allows for real-time monitoring and integration with external systems. API Design While TaktX’s primary API is Kafka itself, client libraries and SDKs provide higher-level abstractions for common operations, making it easier to integrate with various programming languages and frameworks.

title: Job Workers & User Tasks
text: Job Workers and User Tasks TaktX separates job worker and user task processing into distinct topics. This separation enables independent scaling, monitoring, and tuning for each type of workload. Job Worker Topics Each job worker gets its own topic, allowing for dedicated processing and resource allocation. This is especially useful for high-throughput or specialized workers. Using the Kafka consumer group mechansim this also guarantuees that each job is only executed only once. User Task Topic User tasks are passed to a separate topic, enabling dedicated monitoring and processing. This separation also makes it easier to implement custom user interfaces or integrations for human-in-the-loop scenarios. Currently there is no "tasklist" like application. User tasks must be handled using the TatkX client SDK. Scaling and Monitoring By isolating job worker and user task topics, TaktX allows you to scale each independently and monitor their performance separately, ensuring optimal resource usage and responsiveness.

title: Dynamic Topic Management
text: Dynamic Topic Management TaktX is designed to create Kafka topics dynamically as new job workers, user tasks, or process types are introduced. This dynamic approach supports rapid growth and changing workloads, and is a key enabler for horizontal scalability and operational flexibility. Automatic Topic Creation (When Permitted) The engine can automatically create topics on demand, but this depends on the permissions granted by the Kafka operator. In some environments—especially in smaller teams or development setups—Kafka clusters are configured to allow applications to create topics as needed. In these cases, TaktX will detect new workloads and create the necessary topics with the appropriate configuration ( such as partition count and retention policy ) automatically. Enterprise Considerations: Restricted Permissions In larger enterprises, however, Kafka operators often restrict topic creation permissions for security, governance, and operational reasons. It is common for production Kafka clusters to disallow applications from creating topics directly. In these environments, topic management becomes a collaborative process between application teams and Kafka operators. Planned Administration Application To address this, we are planning a dedicated administration application. This tool will help Kafka operators and application teams manage TaktX topics more effectively. The administration app will : Allow operators to review, approve, and create topics manually when automatic creation is not permitted. Optionally, allow controlled topic creation by the administration application when permissions are granted. Provide visibility into existing topics, their configuration, and usage. Support lifecycle management, including topic deletion and reconfiguration. This approach ensures that TaktX can be deployed flexibly in both permissive and tightly controlled Kafka environments, supporting both rapid development and enterprise-grade governance. Operational Flexibility By supporting both automatic and operator-driven topic management, TaktX adapts to a wide range of operational requirements. This enables continuous delivery and rapid iteration in development, while ensuring compliance and control in production.

title: State Management and Persistence
text: State Management and Persistence All process state in TaktX is managed in Kafka Streams state stores. This includes process instances, variables, timers, and message subscriptions. Partitioned State State is partitioned by key ( such as process instance ID ) , allowing for distributed processing and storage. Each engine node is responsible for a subset of the state, based on partition assignment. In-Memory vs. Persisted Stores State stores can be configured for in-memory ( fast, volatile ) or persisted ( durable, larger ) storage. This flexibility allows deployments to be tuned for specific performance and durability requirements. Changelogs and Recovery All state changes are logged to Kafka changelogs. If a node fails, its state can be restored from the changelog, ensuring durability and consistency. Data Retention and Log Compaction A common misconception is that Kafka only retains data for a fixed period ( such as a few days or weeks ) , after which it is deleted. While Kafka does support time-based retention, TaktX relies on Kafka ' s log compaction feature for critical state. Log compaction ensures that for each key ( such as a process instance ID ) , only the most recent value is retained, and older, superseded records are removed. This means that state is not lost by accident : as long as a key is still relevant, its latest value remains available in the log. Data is only deleted from a compacted topic when it has lost its purpose—such as when a process instance is completed and no longer needed. This approach provides strong guarantees against accidental data loss, while keeping storage requirements manageable. Operators can tune compaction and retention policies to match their business and compliance needs.

title: Fault Tolerance and Recovery
text: Fault Tolerance and Recovery TaktX is built for resilience, leveraging Kafka ' s robust fault tolerance mechanisms as its foundation. The default rules and best practices for Kafka fault tolerance apply directly to TaktX deployments. Kafka Replication Factor Kafka topics can be configured with a replication factor, which determines how many copies of each partition are stored across different Kafka brokers. A higher replication factor increases fault tolerance : if a broker fails, another broker with a replica can take over, ensuring no data is lost and the system remains available. For production deployments, we recommend a replication factor of at least 3 for all critical TaktX topics. Acknowledgment (Ack) Settings Both engine nodes and clients can configure the level of acknowledgment required when producing messages to Kafka : acks=1 : The leader broker acknowledges the write as soon as it receives the message. This is fast but less resilient to broker failure. acks=all (recommended): The write is acknowledged only after all in-sync replicas have received the message. This provides the strongest durability guarantees and is recommended for all critical process and state topics in TaktX. Engine Node Recovery If an engine node fails, Kafka Streams automatically restores its state from the changelog topic. Other nodes can take over processing, ensuring minimal disruption. Because all communication is via Kafka, clients and other nodes are unaffected by individual node failures. The combination of Kafka ' s replication and changelog mechanisms ensures that no state is lost and that the system can recover quickly from failures. High Availability By decoupling components and leveraging Kafka’s replication and partitioning, TaktX ensures high availability and fault tolerance across the system. For best results, always monitor broker health, replication status, and consumer lag, and follow Kafka ' s operational best practices for production environments.

title: Scaling and Partitioning
text: Scaling and Partitioning TaktX is designed for horizontal scalability. Both topics and state stores are partitioned, allowing the system to handle increasing workloads by adding more engine nodes and partitions. Partitioning Strategy Kafka’s partitioning ensures that related messages ( e.g., for a specific process instance ) are routed to the same partition, maintaining consistency and enabling parallel processing. However, it is important to note that Kafka only allows partition counts to be increased—not decreased—after topic creation. Increasing the number of partitions can have a significant impact on processing, as it may cause rebalancing and redistribution of data and workload across engine nodes. Because of this, we currently recommend only increasing partition counts when no engine nodes are running. This avoids potential inconsistencies, processing interruptions, or unexpected behavior during rebalancing. Initial Scaling Recommendations For initial deployments, we recommend a partition-to-thread ( CPU core ) ratio of 1 : 1 to 1.5. For example, if you plan to assign 4 to 6 CPU cores or threads to your engine nodes, start with 4 partitions. This ensures efficient resource utilization and balanced workload distribution across engine nodes. Performance Benchmarking For more detailed guidance on sizing and scaling, as well as real-world performance data, please refer to the TaktX performance benchmark documentation Best Practices Monitor partition distribution and consumer lag to ensure optimal performance. Adjust partition counts and node capacity as needed, but always plan partition increases during maintenance windows when no engine nodes are running.

title: Observability and Operations
text: Observability and Operations Observability in TaktX is built on top of Kafka’s robust monitoring ecosystem, complemented by engine-specific metrics exposed via Prometheus. This allows operators to monitor system health, performance, and throughput in real time. Kafka Monitoring Tools Kafka provides a range of built-in tools and metrics for monitoring the health and performance of topics, partitions, and consumers. Key aspects to monitor include : Consumer Lag: This metric shows how far behind a consumer (such as an engine node) is from the latest message in a partition. High consumer lag can indicate processing bottlenecks or resource constraints. Offsets: Kafka tracks the offset of each consumer group for every partition. Monitoring offsets helps ensure that all messages are being processed and none are skipped or stuck. Partition and Broker Health: Kafka exposes metrics on partition leadership, replication status, and broker availability. These are essential for ensuring high availability and fault tolerance. Throughput and Latency: Kafka metrics can be used to monitor message rates, processing latency, and end-to-end throughput, helping you identify performance trends and potential issues. These metrics can be accessed using Kafka’s built-in JMX metrics, command-line tools ( such as kafka-consumer-groups.sh ) , and third-party monitoring solutions like Grafana and Confluent Control Center. Prometheus Metrics TaktX engine nodes expose detailed processing metrics via Prometheus. These metrics provide insight into : Processed event counts and rates Processing durations and latencies State store sizes and access patterns Custom business or workflow metrics (as implemented) Prometheus metrics can be visualized and analyzed using Grafana dashboards, enabling real-time and historical analysis of engine performance. Best Practices Regularly monitor consumer lag and offsets to ensure timely processing and detect bottlenecks early. Set up alerts for partition under-replication, broker failures, or high consumer lag. Use Prometheus and Grafana to visualize engine-specific metrics and correlate them with Kafka-level metrics for a complete operational view.

title: BPMN Feature support
description: What is supported and what not?
text: Although BPMN is an extensive standard, it allows for some vendor specific implementation choices and details. This section and the sections below will describe the supported BPMN concepts and element and how these are implemented by the TaktX engine. The BPMN sections are divided like a class-tree, with real abstract FlowNodeInstance on top and a tree of subclasses. Each subclass adds a specific set of behaviour to the parent class. Some of the concepts and implementation details overarch the specific BPMN classes. These concepts are described in separate sections. These concepts include things like: Error and escalation handling FEEL Expression handling Variable scope handling

title: Element support
description: Supported and not supported elements and concepts
text: The following picture shows the current state of all supported elements: Green : Supported White: Planned for future version Red : Will not be supported Look in the subsections for a detailed overview of all supported elements. The following concepts are currently not (yet) supported: Execution listeners. At this time we believe that this is a concept that should be avoided. It hides complexity and would give a significant performance impact if used. The current implementation of TaktX already allows you to listen to the event stream of everything that happens. The only thing that is not possible is to manipulate variables. DMN Support. Planned for a future release. Connector runtime framework. Planned for a future release. Binding; currently the binding parameter, for example for configuring Call Activities is ignored. The last deployed version is always selected. So when using the Camunda Desktop Modeler make sure to not use these features.

title: Activities
text: BPMN Activities General Concept: BPMN Activities are elements that represent work performed in a process, such as Tasks, Subprocesses, and Call Activities. These elements manage execution, input/output mapping, and variable scoping, ensuring each activity is started, executed, and completed according to BPMN semantics and engine configuration. Usage & Options in TaktX: BPMN Activities in TaktX: Support input and output variable mapping using FEEL expressions for flexible data transformation. Allow for error handling, retries, and compensation, with boundary events for error, escalation, or timer handling. Provide hooks for monitoring, audit logging, and integration with external systems via the TaktX client. Enable advanced features such as multi-instance execution, subprocess invocation, and user assignment. Are specialized into concrete types (service, user, script, call, receive, etc.), each with unique options. We recognise the following Activity subclasses External Tasks : Service task Send task Message End Event Message Intermediate Throw Event Script Tasks User Tasks Call Activities Subprocesses Receive Tasks Generic Tasks Markers Each activity can have markers to add to specialized behaviour: Multi-Instance Activities Compensation (not supported yet)

title: External Tasks
text: External Tasks General Concept: External Tasks in BPMN represent activities that interact with external systems, such as Service Tasks, Send Tasks, and Message Events. These elements manage the execution and integration of work outside the process engine, ensuring correct input/output mapping, error handling, and variable scoping. Typically the work is executed by Job Workers which listen for external tasks to be executed and execute them as soon as they are ready for it. text: Event-Based Gateway General Concept: An Event-Based Gateway in BPMN is used to model branching based on events, where the process waits for one of several possible events to occur before continuing. It is used for event-driven decision points. TaktX Implementation: In TaktX, Event-Based Gateways wait for one of several possible events (message, timer, signal, etc.) and route the process accordingly. The engine manages event subscriptions and variable scope, and resumes the process when an event is caught. Input mappings using FEEL expressions can be used to process event data. Usage & Options in TaktX: An Event-Based Gateway in TaktX allows you to: Wait for one of several possible events (message, timer, signal, etc.) and route the process accordingly. Configure event subscriptions and trigger handling for flexible process routing. Use input mappings to process event data and determine routing. Set up error handling for unmatched or incorrect events. Monitor event handling and audit results via the TaktX client. Use for event-driven process routing and flexible workflows. Example: Customer Response or Timeout with Event-Based Gateway This example shows a process where an Event-Based Gateway waits for either a customer reply (message) or a timeout (timer) and routes accordingly. This demonstrates event-driven process routing in TaktX. Tips & Tricks: Use event-based gateways for flexible, event-driven processes. Document expected events and outcomes. Test gateway behavior with different event scenarios. Pitfalls: Unmatched events will not trigger the process. Incorrect event configuration can block the process. title: Error & Escalation Handling
text: Bubble Up Mechanism & Event Subprocesses in TaktX General Concept: In BPMN, event subprocesses and the bubble up mechanism are essential for robust error and escalation handling. Event subprocesses are triggered by events (error, escalation, message, timer, etc.) and can interrupt or run in parallel to the main flow. The bubble up mechanism describes how errors and escalations propagate through nested scopes until they are caught by an appropriate handler. Event Subprocesses in TaktX Event subprocesses in TaktX are managed on the scope level. When an event occurs, the engine determines the correct scope and starts the event subprocess within that scope. TaktX enforces strict variable scoping, so event subprocesses can access parent variables but can also introduce their own. Event subprocesses can be: Interrupting : Stop the main flow in the scope and start the event subprocess. Used for critical errors or escalations. Non-interrupting : Start the event subprocess in parallel with the main flow. Used for notifications, monitoring, or side effects. Event subprocesses can be triggered by errors, escalations, messages, timers, or signals. They are powerful for exception handling, compensation, and process recovery. Error & Escalation Handling and the Bubble Up Mechanism When an error or escalation is thrown in TaktX, the engine searches for a matching event subprocess or boundary event in the current scope. If not found, the exception "bubbles up" to the parent scope, repeating the search recursively. This continues until the exception is handled or the process instance ends. This mechanism ensures that exceptions are managed according to BPMN semantics, with TaktX-specific enhancements for reliability and clarity. Errors are typically used for unexpected failures. If not caught, they terminate the affected scope and bubble up. Escalations are used for business exceptions or alternative flows. They can be caught by escalation handlers at any level. Both can be caught by event subprocesses or boundary events, either interrupting or non-interrupting. Variable Scoping in Exception Handling Each process, subprocess, and event subprocess in TaktX has its own variable scope. Variables are only visible within their scope unless explicitly mapped. When an error or escalation bubbles up, variable cleanup and compensation are handled automatically. This prevents data leaks and ensures process integrity. Practical Tips for Modeling Robust Processes in TaktX Use interrupting event subprocesses for critical errors that must stop the main flow. Use non-interrupting event subprocesses for monitoring, notifications, or side effects. Always document which errors and escalations can occur and where they are handled. Test your process with both expected and unexpected exceptions to ensure handlers work as intended. Be explicit about variable mappings to avoid accidental data loss or leaks. Use compensation handlers for long-running or transactional activities. Example: Error Escalation and Bubble Up Suppose a subprocess throws an error that is not caught locally. The error bubbles up to the parent process, where an interrupting event subprocess catches it and triggers compensation or an alternative flow. If no handler exists, the process instance ends in error. This ensures that all exceptions are either handled or clearly reported.

title: Variable Handling
text: Variable Handling in TaktX General Concept: Variables in BPMN processes store data and state throughout process execution. In TaktX, variable handling is managed by the ScopeProcessor and Scope classes, ensuring robust scoping, isolation, and mapping between process elements. Scoping Mechanism in TaktX Each process instance, subprocess, and event subprocess in TaktX has its own variable scope. Scopes are organized hierarchically, forming a tree structure. Variables defined in a parent scope are visible to all child scopes (subprocesses, event subprocesses, etc.), but variables defined in a child scope are not visible to the parent or sibling scopes. This ensures data isolation and prevents accidental data leaks or overwrites. Parent-to-Child Visibility: Child scopes can read and use variables from their parent scope. Child-to-Parent Isolation: Parent scopes cannot access variables defined only in a child scope, unless those variables are explicitly mapped out. Explicit Mapping: Input and output mappings (using FEEL expressions) control which variables are passed into or out of a scope. Automatic Cleanup: When a scope ends, its local variables are cleaned up, ensuring no data leaks to other parts of the process. BPMN Example: Variable Scoping Across Subprocess Levels Example Explanation: In this example, the main process defines a variable orderId . The first subprocess ("Payment Subprocess") can access orderId and defines its own variable paymentStatus . A nested subprocess ("Fraud Check Subprocess") can access both orderId and paymentStatus , and defines fraudScore . When the nested subprocess ends, fraudScore is cleaned up unless explicitly mapped out. The parent subprocess and main process cannot access fraudScore unless it is mapped out. This demonstrates the hierarchical visibility and isolation of variables in TaktX. Key Features: Strict variable scoping for each process, subprocess, and event subprocess. Input and output mappings using FEEL expressions. Support for global, local, and transient variables. Automatic cleanup of variables when a scope ends. Isolation between parent and child scopes unless explicitly mapped.

title: FEEL Expressions
text: FEEL Expressions in TaktX General Concept: FEEL (Friendly Enough Expression Language) is a powerful, human-readable expression language designed for business process modeling. In TaktX, FEEL is used to define conditions, calculations, mappings, and logic within BPMN models, making processes more dynamic and adaptable. Introduction to FEEL FEEL is designed to be readable and writable by both business users and developers. It is used to express logic in process conditions, data mappings, and decision tables. FEEL supports a wide range of data types, functions, and operators, making it suitable for complex business logic. Where Can You Use FEEL in TaktX? Gateway Conditions: Decide which path to take in a process based on data. Input/Output Mappings: Transform and map data into and out of tasks, subprocesses, and events. Event Triggers: Define when an event should be triggered based on process data. Loop and Multi-Instance Configuration: Specify collections and logic for repeating activities. Escalation and Error Handling: Express when to throw or catch errors and escalations. FEEL Syntax and Data Types Numbers: 42 , 3.14 Strings: "Hello, world!" Booleans: true , false Lists: [1, 2, 3] , ["A", "B", "C"] Contexts (Maps): {name: "Alice", age: 30} Dates and Times: date("2025-11-08") , time("14:30:00") Operators and Functions Arithmetic: amount + tax , price * quantity Comparison: orderTotal > 1000 , status = "APPROVED" Logical: approved and inStock , not delivered List Operations: count(items) , sum(prices) , all items > 0 Conditional: if score > 80 then "Pass" else "Fail" Accessing Data: customer.address.city , order[1] FEEL Built-in Functions FEEL provides a rich set of built-in functions to help you work with numbers, strings, lists, contexts, dates, and more. These functions make it easy to perform calculations, manipulate data, and express business logic directly in your BPMN models. Below are the main categories and some practical examples: Numeric Functions abs(n): Absolute value. abs(-5) → 5 max(list): Largest value. max([1, 2, 3]) → 3 min(list): Smallest value. min([1, 2, 3]) → 1 sum(list): Total. sum([1, 2, 3]) → 6 round(n, scale): Rounds to decimal places. round(3.1415, 2) → 3.14 String Functions substring(s, start, length): Extracts part of a string. substring("Hello", 2, 3) → ell string length(s): Length of a string. string length("abc") → 3 lower case(s): lower case("ABC") → abc upper case(s): upper case("abc") → ABC contains(s, search): contains("TaktX", "X") → true List Functions count(list): Number of items. count([1,2,3]) → 3 append(list, item): Add item. append([1,2], 3) → [1,2,3] remove(list, item): Remove item. remove([1,2,3], 2) → [1,3] reverse(list): reverse([1,2,3]) → [3,2,1] distinct values(list): distinct values([1,2,2,3]) → [1,2,3] Context Functions get value(context, key): get value({a:1, b:2}, "b") → 2 put(context, key, value): put({a:1}, "b", 2) → {a:1, b:2} keys(context): keys({a:1, b:2}) → ["a", "b"] Date and Time Functions date(string): date("2025-11-08") → 2025-11-08 now(): Current date/time. now() day of week(date): day of week(date("2025-11-08")) → 6 (Saturday) duration(from, to): duration(date("2025-11-08"), date("2025-11-10")) → P2D Boolean and Miscellaneous Functions not(value): Logical negation. not(true) → false is defined(value): Checks if a value is not null. is defined(customer.email) coalesce(a, b, ...): Returns first non-null. coalesce(null, "A", "B") → A For a full list and details, see the Camunda FEEL Built-in Functions Guide . In TaktX, these functions can be used anywhere a FEEL expression is allowed, making your BPMN models more expressive and powerful. Working with Lists and Contexts FEEL makes it easy to work with collections and structured data: List Creation: [1, 2, 3] List Access: orders[2] (second item) List Functions: count(orders) , sum(order.items.price) Context Creation: {name: "Alice", age: 30} Context Access: customer.address.city Conditional Logic FEEL supports if-then-else expressions for decision making: if orderTotal > 1000 then "VIP" else "Standard" Use this to route processes, set variables, or trigger events based on data. Null and Missing Values FEEL handles nulls gracefully. If a variable or property is missing, the result is null . You can check for nulls using is null or is not null : if customer.email is null then "No email" else customer.email Dates and Times Date Creation: date("2025-11-08") Time Creation: time("14:30:00") Date Arithmetic: date("2025-11-08") + duration("P1D") (adds one day) FEEL in Action: Practical Examples 1. Gateway Condition orderAmount > 1000 This expression routes the process down a specific path if the order amount is greater than 1000. 2. Input Mapping for a Subprocess inputCollection: orders Passes the orders list into a multi-instance subprocess. 3. Output Mapping outputElement: processedOrder Maps the result of each instance to processedOrder for aggregation. 4. Escalation Trigger if paymentStatus = "FAILED" then true else false Triggers an escalation if the payment status is "FAILED". 5. Working with Lists sum(order.items.price) Calculates the total price of all items in an order. Tips for Using FEEL in TaktX Keep expressions simple and readable for maintainability. Use FEEL to centralize business logic in your BPMN models. Test expressions with sample data to ensure correctness. Document complex expressions for future reference. Remember that FEEL expressions are evaluated in the context of the current variable scope. Further Reading Camunda FEEL Language Guide Variable Handling in TaktX Event Subprocesses

title: TaktX benchmark results
description: Scalability at a fraction of the cost
text: Benchmark Report: TaktX BPMN Engine TL;DR: Scalability at a fraction of the cost What we measured: TaktX sustained starting ~1,700 PI/s on a “typical” BPMN model (10×200 ms tasks + 2×1-min timers) using just 2×4-vCPU engine nodes and a small 3×2-vCPU broker cluster — with p95 < 500 ms and over 200k concurrent instances at any given time. What it means: That’s ~20–50× higher throughput per node than what teams commonly report for database-centric engines on similar “typical” models. Hitting the same load with TaktX usually means 70–90% fewer cores (and fewer machines), no scale-up RDBMS tier, and simpler ops. This also means that updates are broadcasted in near real-time resulting in very reactive frontend showing the actual process instance state near real time with 100-200ms latency during low loads and still sub-second latency during very high loads. Savings: Compute spend: Cut server counts dramatically to reach the same PI/s. Platform spend: Eliminate relational DB clusters used as workflow backbones. Energy & carbon: Fewer nodes → lower power, cooling, and footprint. Predictable scaling: Add partitions or a small node to scale linearly, instead of costly DB upgrades. Bottom line: Same (or better) SLAs with far less hardware. TaktX drives the €/$ per process instance way down, making high-volume automation economically viable on modest infrastructure. View the subsections for the detailed report. Start at the Introduction

title: Introduction
text: Introduction Business Process Management (BPM) engines are a critical backbone for modern automation platforms, but they are often constrained by performance, scalability, and infrastructure cost. TaktX was built to address these challenges directly: a lean , horizontally scalable and fault tolerant BPMN engine designed from the ground up for high throughput and low latency. This benchmark report presents the first systematic performance results of TaktX under twoscenarios: Raw throughput — a trivial “no wait state” process definition, designed to test the maximumexecution speed of the engine. Sustained throughput — a “typical” business process containing service tasks, timers, and a gateway, designed to represent real-world workloads. The goal of these benchmarks is to demonstrate not only the raw processing ceiling of TaktX, but also its ability to sustain many concurrent process instances with predictable near-real-time latency and near-linear scalability — even on modest cloud infrastructure. It also shows eﬃcient storage; thanks to a compact binary message format and lean persistence, TaktX stores far more instance state per GB than other engines Global architecture of this test Design goal. TaktX is a Kafka-native BPMN engine optimized for high throughput on modest hardware. Execution is fully event-driven; state transitions are written to a durable log and processed in parallel across partitions. By using Kafka we gain the capabilities of a fully horizontally scalable and fault tolerant engine. Core components Engine nodes (stateless compute): Execute BPMN semantics, advance tokens, and emit commands/events. Kafka Streams–based runtime with N threads per node. For this test all local state was stored in memory with the Kafka change-logs as backup. Broker cluster: Kafka cluster with topics for process definition-commands, process instance-commands, timer-schedules, update-stream (broadcast/exports) and change-logs for persistence of state. Note : no other databases are used for processing. Kafka is the only “source of truth” for all engine, worker and other client nodes. Workers: External task executors (for service tasks). In the “typical” benchmark they simulate 200ms work per task. Starter / Load generator: Produces start commands according to a target rate. Observability: Metrics and latency percentiles from engine and workers; optional broadcaststream for UI/analytics. Execution & data flow (simplified) Start. Starter writes StartProcess commands → consumed by an engine node assigned to that partition. Engine step: Engine validates & advances tokens, emits instance update events. Service tasks: Workers consume service task commands, perform work, then emit completed events → engine consumes and advances the token. Timers: Engine writes timer due-dates into timer-schedule (time-bucketed). When buckets elapse, due timers are emitted and processed to resume execution. Completion: Engine writes final state and (optionally) an update on the instance-updates stream. Durability & delivery Writes use acks=all + idempotent producers; engine processing is at-least-once with idempotent state transitions Fault tolerance: If an engine node fails, Kafka partition leadership reassignment + consumer rebalancing moves processing; state is reconstructed from the log and local caches warm quickly. Scalability model Horizontal scale: by increasing partitions and engine nodes. Throughput tracks partition parallelism; adding threads beyond partition count provides no gain. Work isolation: Activities remain bound to the partition that owns their process instance, minimizing cross-partition chatter. Partition per job-worker: Having a separate topic for each job-worker type allows for fine-grained control of scaling partitions. Heavily used job-workers can communicate over topics with more partitions than other less used workers. Security Transport encryption via TLS; credentials via SASL. By fully using Kafka to persist state it becomes very easy to implement end-to-end security for data at rest (planned premium feature). Observability & export cost An optional instance-update broadcast feeds UI/analytics. Disabling it (“running headless”) reduced overhead ~20–30% in the raw tests; sustained tests ran with broadcast on. Why this matters for benchmarks The architecture explains the near-linear scaling with partitions and why latency remains sub-second until saturation. It also clarifies that results were achieved with durability on, and why broadcast slightly lowers the raw ceiling. Next: Raw throughput test

title: Raw Throughput
text: Raw Throughput (No Wait States) Objective The goal of this benchmark was to measure the maximum execution throughput of TaktX on a trivial BPMN process without any wait states. This test represents the upper bound of the engine’s raw performance and scalability. Test setup Kafka: DigitalOcean Managed Cluster (3×2 vCPU Premium), replication factor = 2 Engine nodes: 1 and 2 nodes (4 vCPU, 8GB memory each) Kafka Streams threads: 2–6 per node Process starter: 1 node, 4 vCPU, 1 thread Durability: acks=all, idempotence=true Other: Kafka batch=262,144, linger=50 ms, commit interval=100 ms, poll=50 ms Tests were run by starting 1,000,000 process instances as fast as possible. I measured the time until no more consumer lag was visible indicating that all process instances were finished. Results Key takeaways: Single-node ceiling (with broadcast): ~71k PI/s @ 6 partitions, 6 streams threads, 4 client threads. Two-node scaling: With 12 partitions, ~111k PI/s (broadcast on). That’s a strong scale-up over the 1-node result, limited mainly by Kafka/partition parallelism rather than CPU. Headless mode: Turning oﬀ exports/broadcast lifts this to ~143k PI/s on the same 2-node setup, showing that observability adds measurable but moderate overhead. Threads vs partitions: At 3 partitions, increasing Streams threads from 4 → 6 doesn’t help (same 62.5k PI/s), confirming the partition count was the limiter there. Gains resume when moving to 6 and 12 partitions. Durability still on: Even with acks=all and idempotence=true, throughput remains six-figure PI/s on modest hardware. Next: Sustained throughput test

title: Sustained throughput
description: Starting process instances at a sustained rate
text: Sustained throughput Objective The goal of this benchmark was to find the maximum number of sustained starting process instances per second of a “typical” process definition. This gives an indication of a “real world scenario” performance. We want to know the amount of process instances that can be handled concurrently and want to find out the latency numbers between messages passed and processed. Note : Note: this model is similar in shape (multiple tasks, timers, gateway) to the ‘typical’ process used in Camunda performance posts The typical process definition consists of 10 service tasks. Each worker takes a dummy 200ms to complete. Each service task executes a simple FEEL expression to dynamically determine the job worker id. Furthermore there are two timers of 1 minute each and a gateway is also included. This means the theoretical duration of a process instance is 2x 1 minute + 10x200ms = 122 seconds. Each instance is started with the following variable payload of approximately 100 bytes: Test setup Two tests were performed using the same Kafka cluster of 3x2CPU with 8GB memory each. The first run was with 1 engine node and the second run was with 2 engine nodes. Partitions: 12 Threads: 6 for each node Worker and starter node: 4CPU, 2 threads for workers Durability: acks=all, idempotence=true, broadcast updates = true Other: Kafka batch=262,144, linger=50 ms, commit interval=100 ms, poll=50 ms Latency is measured as the time passed between the producing of a Kafka message and the reception and processing on another node For each run, we slowly increased the number of process instances started. After each increase we waited until the increased number of process instances started to finish. This explains the “staircase” for the process instance throughput. I kept increasing the number of jobs until the latency “exploded” indicating the engine or Kafka could no longer keep up. Results with 1 engine node Graph Analysis Process instance throughput (bottom-left graph): Shows the staircase ramp-up of process start rates. Sustained throughput climbs to over 850 PI/s before instability appears. Flow Object throughput (bottom-right graph): Peaks around 12,500 flow nodes per second, matching the expected factor (10 service tasks + 2 timers + gateway per process). Latency percentiles (top graphs): Stable phase: P50 latency stays around 200–300 ms, P95 and P99 under 500 ms. Saturation point (~11:15): Latencies shoot up, with P99 exceeding 800 ms, showing the engine or Kafka reached max sustainable throughput. Process duration (top-middle graph): Average process duration aligns closely with the theoretical 122 s baseline during stable load with a value of around 124 seconds. This aligns nicely with the given latencies, confirming timers and worker delays are respected. At overload, average duration rises slightly before leveling out. Process instance totals (bottom-middle graph): Over 1 million instances were started and finished, with both “started” and “finished” lines tracking steadily — until the overload point, where completion lagged. At peak there were over 100,000 active processes being maintained by the single engine node. Results with 2 engine nodes Note : Above graph is for 1 node, so the throughput numbers should be doubled: Throughput: Plateaued around ~1,600–1,700 PI/s per cluster (each node contributing ~800–850 PI/s, graphs show per-node throughput). Almost doubling showing horizontal scalability Latency: P50 remained ~200–250 ms P95 ~400–500 ms P99 ~600–800 ms Even at doubled throughput, latency profiles were almost identical to the 1-node run. Process duration: Again stable around theoretical baseline, showing that scaling horizontally does not aﬀect business-level timing. Scaling behavior: Throughput nearly doubled when moving from 1 → 2 nodes, proving linear scalability for this workload. Next: cpu and memory usage

title: CPU / Memory usage
description: CPU / Memory usage of engine and Kafka nodes
text: Engine loads; test started around 12:15, we see a slowly increasing CPU load and a slowly increasing memory consumption due to the number of active process instances in memory. Due to the the compact in-memory representation of process instance state memory consumption is relatively small. Kafka: It seems that we reached the part where the engine nodes becomes the bottleneck. At a certain point Kafka cpu usage does not increase anymore. So probably by adding another engine node we could have even scaled up further. Conclusion In this sustained benchmark with a “typical” BPMN process (10 service tasks, 200 ms each, 2 timers of 1 minute), TaktX demonstrated both high throughput and stable latency at scale. With one engine node, throughput plateaued around 850 PI/s (~12k flow nodes/s) while sustaining over 100,000 concurrent active processes with sub-second latency (p95 ~400–500 ms). With two engine nodes, throughput scaled nearly linearly to ~1,700 PI/s (~24k flow nodes/s) with over 200,000 concurrent processes — without any meaningful increase in latency. Process durations tracked the theoretical 122 s baseline, confirming timers and workers were correctly orchestrated under load. These results highlight that TaktX is not only capable of extreme raw throughput (as shown in Scenario 1), but also delivers predictable, real-world sustained performance with millions of concurrent long-running process instances — while maintaining linear scalability across nodes. Next: storage efficiency

title: Storage efficiency
text: Storage efficiency The messages being passed around and persisted are binary formatted and tiny. There are several points where data is passed around or persisted: Process execution administration: keeps a working record of a process instance required to further process it. This is persisted in Kafka Topics and changelogs in the Kafka cluster for all process instances until they have been completed after which the data is purged. The engine nodes keep these cached in memory. After a restart the memory is restored from the changelogs Output stream: this is a stream of data representing what happened to process instances and flow nodes and can be read by consumers with specific purposes. This data is retained for a configurable period of time. For example for the process definitions used in this test this was the amount of data persisted in the Kafka cluster: For the minimal trivial process definition: Process execution administration: 100 bytes per process instance Output stream: 400 bytes per finished process instance For the “typical” process definition (started with approximately 100 byte variable payload) Process execution administration: 9kB Output stream: 3kB If we take the “typical” process definition; what this eﬀectively means is that an engine node with 8GB of memory is theoretically able to administer and process over 900,000 active process instances in memory at any one time. If we need more we can add nodes but we can also choose to persist to disk allowing for much more at the cost of a bit performance. For running instances a single Kafka node with a 150GB disk could store process instance information for over 13 million active process instances (including the output stream). So with a cluster of three that would increase to around 40 million. Kafka will remove old/stale data after a configurable retention period. When configured correctly this will eﬀectively increase that number even more. Next: Compared to others

title: Compared to others
text: Comparison with other BPMN engines When the process model contains multiple tasks, timers, and gateway logic, database and coordination overheads dominate. Below we contrast sustained, realistic workloads and consider resources required to reach the reported numbers. TaktX (this report). Model: 10 service tasks (200 ms each), 2×1-minute timers, 1 gateway Cluster: DigitalOcean managed Kafka 3×2 vCPU (RF=2); engines: 1–2 nodes, 4 vCPU each; workers/starter: 4 vCPU. Result: ~850 PI/s (1 node) → ~1,700 PI/s (2 nodes) with p95 < 500 ms, up to ~2M concurrent instances; near-linear scaling from one to two engine nodes. Camunda / Zeebe “typical” in practice (community evidence). In field reports for Camunda, realistic models with timers and external tasks frequently plateau around ~30–40 PI/s unless significantly larger clusters and heavy tuning are applied. This aligns with the known cost of job executor/database contention on such workloads. Context & normalization: Against that backdrop, TaktX’s ~850–1,700 PI/s on small engine nodes and a tiny Kafka cluster represents a 20–50× uplift in sustained throughput for “typical” models, with sub-second p95 latency. Flowable 6.3.0 – oﬃcial benchmark (public). Flowable published a performance benchmark showing “close to 10,000 process instances per second (9,541 to be precise), each one executing 10 service tasks” on AWS. This is a light per-instance workload (no minute-long timers and no intentional 200 ms task delays), but it is still a useful public reference for realistic multi-task models. Context & normalization: My TaktX raw test (no waits) exceeds 100,000 PI/s, i.e., >10× Flowable’s figure on modest hardware; on the typical test (with two minute-level timers and 200 ms workers), TaktX still sustains ~1.7k PI/s on two 4-vCPU nodes — despite the much heavier per-instance work. (Flowable’s post does not include long timers or fixed per-task delays.) jBPM jBPM publishes base performance numbers measured through KIE Server, which means results include network and marshalling overhead in addition to the engine itself. Their page reports throughput scaling with client threads, e.g. ~91 process instances/sec with 1 thread and ~240 instances/sec with 4 threads (with further gains at higher thread counts on that page). How this maps to our “typical” model: My sustained test (10 service tasks at 200 ms each, two 1-minute timers, gateway) reaches ~850 PI/s on one 4-vCPU engine node and ~1,700 PI/s on two nodes, with p95 < 500 ms and ≈2 M concurrent instances—despite much heavier per-instance work and end-to-end durability (acks=all, idempotent, broadcast updates). Even allowing for KIE Server overhead in jBPM’s numbers, the order-of-magnitude gap remains: TaktX delivers significantly higher sustained PI/s on modest hardware for realistic, timer-rich flows. Notes on comparability: jBPM’s published tests are executed over KIE Server (remote calls +marshalling), whereas my runs use a Kafka-backed architecture with workers and timers inside themodel. The raw numbers aren’t apples-to-apples, but normalizing for resources and model weight still shows a substantial advantage for TaktX on sustained “typical” workloads Takeaway (typical-process focus): Throughput per node / per vCPU: TaktX delivers ≈850 PI/s per 4-vCPU engine node on a heavy, timer-rich model — with durability (acks=all, idempotent producers) and exports on. Infra required to reach target rates: Where other engines often require larger broker fleets or beefy DB tiers to stay above a few dozen PI/s on realistic models, TaktX hits ~1.7k PI/s on two small nodes plus a 3-broker Kafka. Latency under load: TaktX maintains p95 < 500 ms until saturation, whereas forum evidence for other engines shows latency pressure already in the tens of PI/s. Notes on comparability. No two public benchmarks are perfectly identical. Flowable’s 6.3.0 test uses 10 service tasks but no minute-level timers and no enforced per-task delays; Camunda forum figures reflect real installations rather than staged lab runs. The comparisons above therefore normalize qualitatively for model weight and resources rather than claiming strict apples-to-apples parity. Still, the magnitude of the deltas is clear. Next: Conclusion

title: Conclusion
text: In this sustained benchmark with a “typical” BPMN process (10 service tasks, 200 ms each, 2 timers of 1 minute), TaktX demonstrated both high throughput and stable latency at scale. With one engine node, throughput plateaued around 850 PI/s (~12k flow nodes/s) while sustaining 100k+ concurrent active processes with sub-second latency (p95 ~400–500 ms). With two engine nodes, throughput scaled nearly linearly to ~1,700 PI/s (~24k flow nodes/s) with 200k+ concurrent processes — without any meaningful increase in latency. Process durations tracked the theoretical 122 s baseline, confirming timers and workers were correctly orchestrated under load. Beyond raw performance, these results translate directly into cost eﬃciency. Achieving this level of throughput on just 2×4-vCPU engine nodes (plus a small 3-broker cluster) means materially fewer cores and fewer machines to reach a given PI/s target, no heavyweight scale-up RDBMS tier acting as a bottleneck, and therefore lower cloud spend (compute and storage), simpler operations, and a smaller energy footprint . In practical terms, teams can meet or raise SLAs with far less hardware, cutting recurring infrastructure costs while keeping latency predictable. TaktX is not only capable of extreme raw throughput (Scenario 1) but also delivers real-world, sustained performance with linear scalability — turning high-volume automation into a performance-per-euro advantage.
